egm-dai-001.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). Remote monitoring sends a "therapy delivered" alert; contacted by phone, the patient felt nothing. How do you interpret this episode?
options: Sinus tachycardia with 1:1 conduction, inappropriately treated with ATP
1:1 AVNRT, terminated by the ATP delivered
Monomorphic VT dissociated from the atria, terminated by ATP
Rapid AF conducted into the VT zone, ATP ineffective
commentaires: Incorrect: in sinus tachycardia, every V is preceded by an A at the same rate; here there are far more Vs than As.
Incorrect: AVNRT gives a 1:1 relationship (or A ≥ V); here the atria beat at 75 bpm while the ventricles beat at 180 bpm.
Correct: regular V cycle length of 330 ms, independent sinus atrial activity at 800 ms (V > A), then return to sinus rhythm immediately after the 8 pulses.
Incorrect: the atrial EGM shows regular sinus P waves at 800 ms, not rapid disorganised activity.
egm-dai-001.explication: The first step in reading an ICD episode is to count As and Vs and look at their relationship. Here, the atrial channel shows sinus P waves at 800 ms (75 bpm) unrelated to the regular ventricular activity at 330 ms (≈ 180 bpm): there are more Vs than As, which indicates VT in the vast majority of cases. The ICD detects in the VT zone (TS then TD), delivers an 8-pulse ATP sequence, and sinus rhythm resumes immediately: the therapy is appropriate and effective. The pitfall is to conclude that therapy was inappropriate because the patient felt nothing: ATP is painless, which is precisely its advantage. Rule of thumb: count As and Vs, then check what happens immediately after the therapy.
egm-dai-001.aRetenir: More Vs than As and return to sinus rhythm immediately after ATP: VT treated appropriately and effectively.

egm-dai-002.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). Reviewing this episode, which feature most reliably establishes the diagnosis of VT?
options: Ventricular activity faster than atrial activity
A ventricular rate well above 170 bpm
The perfect regularity of the ventricular cycles at 330 ms
Termination of the tachycardia by the ATP delivered
commentaires: Correct: V > A (dissociation) indicates VT in the vast majority of cases; the exceptions (junctional tachycardia with retrograde block) are rare.
Incorrect: rate alone does not distinguish VT from SVT; sinus tachycardia or AF can reach these rates.
Incorrect: an SVT (2:1 flutter, re-entry) is also perfectly regular; regularity mainly rules out AF.
Incorrect: ATP can also terminate a re-entrant SVT or flutter; its success does not prove a ventricular origin.
egm-dai-002.explication: The most robust criterion for classifying an episode on a dual-chamber ICD is the A/V relationship. When Vs outnumber As, as here (V at 330 ms, sinus A at 800 ms), the diagnosis of VT is almost certain. Rate and regularity do not discriminate: sinus tachycardia, 2:1 flutter or re-entry are equally fast and regular. Termination by ATP is a weak argument, because ATP also terminates re-entrant SVTs. Rule of thumb: always start with the A/V relationship before assessing morphology or the response to therapy.
egm-dai-002.aRetenir: On a dual-chamber EGM, V > A = VT until proven otherwise; the response to ATP proves nothing.

egm-dai-003.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). The resident asks you what type of ATP was delivered during this episode. What do you tell them?
options: A ramp of 8 pulses whose cycle length shortens by 10 ms with each pulse
Rapid atrial pacing at 88% of the cycle length, to capture the atrium
A train of 8 pulses set at 88% of the 800 ms sinus atrial cycle length
A fixed-cycle burst of 8 pulses at about 88% of the VT cycle length
commentaires: Incorrect: in a ramp, the intervals shorten from pulse to pulse; here, successive pulses remain 290 ms apart.
Incorrect: ATP is delivered on the ventricular channel (TP below the line), not to the atrium.
Incorrect: ATP is calculated from the ventricular tachycardia cycle length, not the atrial cycle length.
Correct: after the first pulse, the TP markers follow one another every 290 ms, i.e. 88% of the 330 ms cycle length: this is a burst.
egm-dai-003.explication: The TP markers show 8 ventricular pulses delivered at a fixed cycle length of 290 ms, i.e. 88% of the VT cycle length (330 ms): this is burst ATP, the scheme validated by PainFREE Rx II and offered by default by most manufacturers. A ramp is recognised by intervals that shorten within the sequence. Ventricular ATP is always calculated from the VT cycle length, never from the atrial cycle length. Rule of thumb: read the intervals between therapy markers to identify the scheme delivered before changing it.
egm-dai-003.aRetenir: Identical TP intervals = burst; shortening intervals = ramp.

egm-dai-004.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). Contacted by phone, the patient feels well. This is the first episode since implantation. Which actions are appropriate?
options: Replace ATP with an immediate shock, as ATP may accelerate the VT
Send him to the emergency department for a precautionary external shock
Check the beta-blocker dose and arrange an early clinic review
Raise the VT zone to 200 bpm to avoid further therapies
Look for a trigger: potassium, ischaemia, decompensation, adherence
commentaires: Incorrect: ATP painlessly terminates most monomorphic VTs; the risk of acceleration is low and covered by the subsequent shock.
Incorrect: the VT has terminated and the patient is in sinus rhythm; an external shock makes no sense.
Correct: optimising background therapy and an early review are the logical next steps after an effectively treated VT.
Incorrect: a zone at 200 bpm would leave his clinical VT (≈ 180 bpm) untreated.
Correct: any treated VT should prompt a search for a correctable precipitating factor.
egm-dai-004.explication: A VT terminated by ATP in an asymptomatic patient does not warrant emergency care, but it must not be dismissed: a precipitating factor should be sought (hypokalaemia, ischaemia, worsening heart failure, beta-blocker discontinuation) and treatment reviewed. The pitfalls are overreacting (emergency department, external shock) or reprogramming in the wrong direction: raising the zone above the clinical VT rate would make it invisible, and removing ATP would expose the patient to avoidable shocks. In secondary prevention, the slowest zone stays below the documented VT rate. Rule of thumb: VT terminated by ATP = look for the cause and optimise treatment, without touching what works.
egm-dai-004.aRetenir: VT terminated by ATP in a patient who is well: look for the cause, optimise treatment, do not switch off ATP.

egm-dai-005.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). True or false: in this episode, the success of ATP alone establishes that this was VT and not SVT.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: ATP can also terminate supraventricular re-entry or flutter; it is not a diagnostic criterion.
Correct: it is the V > A dissociation seen before ATP that makes the diagnosis, not the response to therapy.
egm-dai-005.explication: The decisive argument on this tracing is the A/V relationship: the ventricles beat at 330 ms while the atria remain in sinus rhythm at 800 ms. Termination by ATP confirms that the therapy was effective, not the mechanism: AVNRT, accessory pathway re-entry or flutter can also be terminated by rapid ventricular pacing. The reverse pitfall also applies: failed ATP does not rule out VT. Rule of thumb: make the diagnosis on the EGMs before the therapy (A/V relationship, morphology, onset), then judge efficacy afterwards.
egm-dai-005.aRetenir: The diagnosis is made on the EGMs before therapy; the response to ATP does not classify the rhythm.

egm-dai-006.question: A 67-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease (LVEF 30%) has a dual-chamber ICD implanted for secondary prevention after a monomorphic VT at 170 bpm. VT zone programmed at 375 ms (160 bpm) with ATP then shocks; VF zone at 250 ms (240 bpm). This patient has had four identical episodes in one month, all terminated by the first ATP sequence despite an adequate beta-blocker dose. A colleague suggests setting the VT zone to "monitor only" to spare him these therapies. What is the best approach?
options: Set the VT zone to monitor only, as the VF zone is enough to protect him
Keep ATP and consider an antiarrhythmic drug or VT ablation
Replace ATP with an immediate shock, which is safer if VT recurs
Lower the VT zone to 130 bpm to treat VTs earlier
commentaires: Incorrect: a VT at 180 bpm is below the VF zone (240 bpm); with monitoring only, it would no longer be treated at all.
Correct: recurrent monomorphic VT in an ICD patient should prompt consideration of antiarrhythmic escalation or ablation, while keeping the effective therapy.
Incorrect: an immediate shock exposes the patient to avoidable painful shocks when ATP terminates these VTs every time.
Incorrect: such a low zone captures exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and AF, causing inappropriate therapies.
egm-dai-006.explication: Recurrent monomorphic VT, even when successfully terminated by ATP, reflects an active substrate: the 2022 ESC guidelines recommend considering VT ablation (or antiarrhythmic escalation, particularly amiodarone) in ICD patients with recurrences. Setting the VT zone to monitor only would leave a VT at 180 bpm untreated, since it lies below the VF zone: this is a classic and dangerous "de-escalation" pitfall. Replacing ATP with a shock or lowering the zone would increase shocks, whether appropriate or not. Rule of thumb: when ATP works, keep it, and treat the substrate.
egm-dai-006.aRetenir: Recurrent VT terminated by ATP: keep ATP and treat the substrate (antiarrhythmic drug, ablation).

egm-dai-007.question: A 59-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) has a dual-chamber ICD for primary prevention. Her husband found her on the floor; she regained consciousness within a few seconds and complains of having "been kicked in the chest". In the emergency department, you interrogate the ICD. How do you interpret this episode?
options: Lead noise detected in the VF zone, inappropriate shock
VF detected in the VF zone, charge then effective shock
Fast monomorphic VT terminated by ATP during charging
Rapid AF conducted into the VF zone, inappropriate shock
commentaires: Incorrect: lead noise appears only on the RV EGM; here the shock EGM also shows the VF.
Correct: rapid, disorganised ventricular activity (cycle lengths ≈ 200–240 ms) on both the RV EGM and the shock EGM, charging, shock, then pacing.
Incorrect: the activity is polymorphic and irregular, and no ATP marker appears; it was terminated by a shock.
Incorrect: the ventricular activity itself is disorganised on both ventricular channels; these are not conducted QRS complexes.
egm-dai-007.explication: The episode shows an abrupt transition from sinus rhythm to rapid, polymorphic, disorganised ventricular activity, visible on both the RV EGM and the shock EGM: this is VF, detected in the VF zone (FS markers). The ICD charges its capacitors (Chg) while the VF persists, then delivers a shock (CD) that terminates it. The shock is therefore appropriate and effective, and the syncope is explained by the VF itself. The pitfall is to conclude too quickly that very rapid signals are lead noise: noise remains confined to the RV EGM, whereas VF is seen on all ventricular channels. Rule of thumb: always compare the RV EGM with the shock EGM.
egm-dai-007.aRetenir: Disorganised activity on the RV EGM AND the shock EGM = true VF; confined to the RV EGM = noise.

egm-dai-008.question: A 59-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) has a dual-chamber ICD for primary prevention. Her husband found her on the floor; she regained consciousness within a few seconds and complains of having "been kicked in the chest". The ward nurse asks you what the last events marked VP, at the end of the recording, correspond to. What do you tell her?
options: Asynchronous safety pacing imposed after every shock delivered
Consolidation ATP delivered automatically after termination
Pacing of a residual slow VT not recognised by the ICD
Post-shock backup pacing, pending return of an intrinsic rhythm
commentaires: Incorrect: the VPs are about 1000 ms apart (60 bpm) and there is no sign of asynchronous pacing; this is bradycardia pacing.
Incorrect: ATP is fast (cycle length close to that of the VT); pulses at 60 bpm are bradycardia pacing.
Incorrect: each VP is followed by a paced complex, with no underlying tachycardia; there is no residual VT.
Correct: after a shock, the intrinsic rhythm may be depressed; the ICD provides backup pacing, often at increased output, according to the post-shock programming.
egm-dai-008.explication: After a shock, the sinus node and conduction may be transiently stunned. ICDs provide post-shock bradycardia pacing, programmable in rate, amplitude and duration, often at increased output to ensure capture of shocked myocardium. The VPs at 1000 ms (60 bpm) correspond to this normal function. The pitfall is to interpret them as an additional antitachycardia therapy or as a sensing problem. Rule of thumb: after a shock, check for the return of an intrinsic rhythm and for capture during post-shock pacing.
egm-dai-008.aRetenir: Slow VPs immediately after a shock = post-shock pacing, normal device function.

egm-dai-009.question: A 59-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) has a dual-chamber ICD for primary prevention. Her husband found her on the floor; she regained consciousness within a few seconds and complains of having "been kicked in the chest". She is now conscious, in sinus rhythm, and asks to go home. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Admit her to look for an acute cause (ischaemia, electrolytes, HF)
Discharge her: the shock was effective, follow-up in three months
Switch off shocks to spare her further trauma
Start a class IC antiarrhythmic drug and discharge her
commentaires: Correct: VF with syncope requires a search for an acute cause (acute coronary syndrome, electrolyte disturbance, decompensation) and a review of treatment.
Incorrect: an effective shock does not remove the need to find out why the VF occurred.
Incorrect: this is precisely the therapy that has just saved her life; switching it off would be a serious error.
Incorrect: class IC antiarrhythmic drugs are contraindicated in heart disease with LV dysfunction.
egm-dai-009.explication: An appropriate shock for VF with loss of consciousness is not "just a shock": it is a cardiac arrest from which the patient was rescued by the ICD. She should be admitted to look for an acute cause (ischaemia, potassium disturbance, heart failure decompensation, drug-related factor), treatment should be optimised, and driving restrictions required by regulations should be discussed. Sending the patient home because "the ICD did its job" is the pitfall of underreaction. Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs are contraindicated in structural heart disease. Rule of thumb: shock with syncope, chest pain or multiple shocks = hospital admission.
egm-dai-009.aRetenir: Appropriate shock with syncope = admission and search for a cause, even if everything is back to normal.

egm-dai-010.question: A 59-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) has a dual-chamber ICD for primary prevention. Her husband found her on the floor; she regained consciousness within a few seconds and complains of having "been kicked in the chest". True or false: an appropriate and effective shock, as in this episode, has no prognostic value of its own: it simply shows that the ICD works.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: shocks, both appropriate and inappropriate, are associated with increased mortality in heart failure patients (SCD-HeFT).
Correct: an appropriate shock is a marker of the severity of the heart disease and should prompt a reassessment of overall management.
egm-dai-010.explication: In the SCD-HeFT analysis (Poole, 2008), patients who received an appropriate shock had markedly higher mortality than those without shocks, and inappropriate shocks were also associated with increased mortality. An appropriate shock is therefore a marker of disease progression (and possibly an aggravating factor), not simply a "successful test" of the ICD. This is one of the reasons why modern programming aims to avoid unnecessary shocks (ATP, prolonged detection duration). Rule of thumb: after a shock, reassess heart failure, ischaemia and background therapy.
egm-dai-010.aRetenir: A shock, even an appropriate one, is a warning sign that requires reassessment of the heart disease.

egm-dai-011.question: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has a dual-chamber ICD implanted in 2014 for primary prevention. The programming has never been reviewed: VT zone at 133 bpm (450 ms) with ATP then shocks, discriminators off. Remote monitoring reports an episode in the VT zone. How do you interpret this episode?
options: Polymorphic VT with retrograde conduction to the atrium
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction, correctly classified in the VT zone
AF with a rapid, irregular ventricular response, misclassified as VT
Monomorphic VT coexisting with AF (dual tachycardia)
commentaires: Incorrect: the ventricular EGMs keep a narrow, constant morphology from one cycle to the next, and the atrium is faster than the ventricle.
Incorrect: 2:1 flutter gives regular Vs; here the V cycle lengths vary from 300 to 440 ms.
Correct: rapid, disorganised atrial activity, irregular Vs between 300 and 440 ms, identical morphology on the initial VS events and the TS events: conducted AF.
Incorrect: in dual tachycardia, the VT is regular and has a different morphology; here the Vs are irregular and unchanged.
egm-dai-011.explication: The atrial EGM shows rapid, disorganised activity (A-A intervals from 140 to 215 ms): this is AF. The ventricles follow irregularly (300 to 440 ms), with an identical morphology on the first VS events and on the cycles classified as TS. The ICD classifies these cycles in the VT zone only because the zone is programmed very low (133 bpm) and the discriminators are off: this is false VT detection, a classic cause of inappropriate therapy. The pitfall is to read "VT" on the counter without looking at the EGMs. Rule of thumb: A faster than V + irregular Vs + unchanged morphology = conducted AF.
egm-dai-011.aRetenir: A > V, irregular Vs and unchanged morphology: AF conducted into the VT zone, not VT.

egm-dai-012.question: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has a dual-chamber ICD implanted in 2014 for primary prevention. The programming has never been reviewed: VT zone at 133 bpm (450 ms) with ATP then shocks, discriminators off. Remote monitoring reports an episode in the VT zone. Which features of this tracing identify inappropriate detection of AF?
options: Onset with a PVC followed by abrupt acceleration
Marked irregularity of the ventricular cycles
Atrial activity faster than ventricular activity
Dissociation with more Vs than As
Ventricular EGMs of the same morphology on the VS and TS events
commentaires: Incorrect: the episode does not start with a PVC; AF is present from the start of the recording.
Correct: the V cycle lengths vary from 300 to 440 ms, an irregularity typical of AF.
Correct: A > V is the profile of a conducted atrial tachyarrhythmia, here AF.
Incorrect: it is the opposite; V > A would point towards VT.

Correct: the first VS events and the TS events have the same morphology on the RV EGM and the shock EGM, favouring supraventricular conduction (to be confirmed by comparison with the template recorded in sinus rhythm).
egm-dai-012.explication: Three classic features, readable without any algorithm, point to conducted AF: the A/V relationship (A faster than V), irregular ventricular cycles and a ventricular morphology that does not change from beat to beat (and, for the discriminator, matches the sinus rhythm template). These are precisely the criteria used by the discriminators (A/V relationship, stability, morphology). Conversely, an abrupt onset with a PVC and V > A dissociation would favour VT. Rule of thumb: for any "VT" episode, check these three criteria before calling the therapy appropriate.
egm-dai-012.aRetenir: A/V relationship, regularity and morphology: the three keys to unmasking AF classified as VT.
